To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
We propose a theoretically founded approach for spectral analysis of electroanatomical maps (EAM), to determine the minimum number spatial EGM required for accurate EAM.
we proposed a theoretically founded method to estimate spatial bandwidth in EAM from CNS, and we demonstrated that it depends on the EAM quality.
we propose a theoretically grounded method for spectral representation of EAM in terms of spatial frequency from manifold harmonics analysis (MHA).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the spectral analysis of EAM to estimate the spatial bandwidth for accurate EAM reconstruction.
the spectral analysis of the EAM, which is a key step to determine the minimum spatial bandwidth for EAM, and to provide support to ablation.
the theoretical and experimental analysis of the EAM spectrum, providing a methodological framework to support the spatial bandwidth estimation and the EAM reconstruction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the proposed spectral analysis of EAM provides a useful support to ablation, as it allows to estimate the spatial bandwidth required for accurate reconstruction of anatomical meshes, and EAM in terms of the underlying arrhythmia mechanism.
the proposed method is a valuable tool in order to estimate the minimum number of electrodes required for accurate EAM, which could be used to support ablation in clinical practice.

the proposed approach can be used to estimate the spatial sampling rate required to obtain accurate EAM for a specific arrhythmia mechanism, which could be used to optimize the number of EGM to register for ablation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
MHA can be used to estimate the minimum number of spatial EGM for accurate EAM reconstruction in CNS, accounting for both anatomical and bioelectric features.
MHA provides an accurate estimation for spatial sampling rate and bandwidth in EAM, and a theoretically founded spectrum representation for EAM spatial features.
MHA can provide a theoretically-founded method to estimate the spatial bandwidth of EAM, and to determine the minimum number and positions for EGM sampling.
The main takeaway from our work is that
MHA provides the spectrum representation of the spatial features, allowing to estimate the minimum number of points for accurate EAM.
the proposed MHA spectrum can be used as a support to ablation by providing the minimum number of electrodes to register EGM for obtaining accurate EAM with an estimated spatial bandwidth.
the spatial sampling rate can be estimated by MHA and the cut-off spatial bandwidth can be computed from the spectrum magnitude of the anatomical and the bioelectrical features in the EAM.
